messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 41-year-old man who works the fry station at a busy fast-food restaurant in a strip mall on the outskirts of Detroit. He came to therapy at the urging of his manager, who had noticed Amir flinching and dropping utensils whenever the drive-thru headset crackled or a coworker slammed a freezer door. Amir is single and lives alone in a basement apartment he chose specifically because it is below ground and quiet.

The event that changed everything happened three years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. Amir was standing at the back of a convenience store, waiting to pay for a soda, when a man in a ski mask burst through the door and fired a handgun twice. The first shot hit the clerk in the chest. The second hit a display of potato chips. Amir remembers the sound more than the image—the percussive crack, the way it seemed to split the air inside his skull. He dropped to the floor and stayed there, frozen, until the shooter ran out and the sirens started. He was not injured, but he never made it back to work that day. He never went into that convenience store again.

In the months that followed, Amir found himself increasingly watchful. He began to notice that his body went tight at certain moments without his permission. The worst moments came at the same time of day the shooting had occurred—mid-afternoon, between two and three. He would feel his heart speed up for no reason he could name, and he would start scanning the room for exits. When a customer at the restaurant raised their voice to complain about an order, Amir felt the same surge of alarm he had felt when the man in the mask had shouted. He had come to believe that being criticised meant something dangerous was about to happen—that the person was about to escalate, that he needed to be ready. A manager correcting his fry portion made his hands shake. A coworker saying "you messed up the ticket" sent a bolt of cold fear through his chest.

Amir began to avoid the time of day the shooting had occurred. He asked his manager to schedule him only for morning shifts, and when that was not always possible, he started calling in sick on afternoons he could not trade away. His paychecks shrank. He stopped going to the grocery store after two o'clock. He stopped answering his phone between two and three, because the ringtone itself had become a trigger—a sudden noise that yanked him back to the crack of the gun. He was on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds, and he had learned to move through his apartment in near-silence, wincing at the clatter of a dropped spoon.

The only place Amir felt safe was his basement apartment. He had come to believe that nowhere else was truly secure. When the bus ran late, he assumed something bad was happening—an accident, a shooting, a reason for the delay that would confirm his worst fears. He would stand at the bus stop, jaw clenched, watching the street for signs of trouble. He had stopped taking the bus altogether on afternoons. He walked to work, even when it took forty minutes, because at least he could see what was coming.

What finally brought Amir to therapy was a moment he could not explain away. A customer had tapped him on the shoulder to ask for ketchup, and Amir had spun around so violently that he knocked a tray of fries onto the floor. The customer had stepped back, hands up, saying "whoa, man, I just wanted ketchup." Amir had stood there, trembling, unable to speak. His manager had pulled him aside afterward and told him he needed help. Amir agreed, not because he thought therapy would work, but because he had run out of places to hide. What frightens him most is the possibility that the feeling will never stop—that he will spend the rest of his life jumping at sounds and waiting for something bad to happen, trapped in his basement with his own alarm.
